title: Bagging and Bootstrap Aggregation
abstract:
Bagging — Bootstrap AGGregatING — trains the same algorithm many times on
different random samples of the data and averages the results. This document
covers the two halves of the name, the mathematics of bootstrap sampling
(including the $1/e$ result that leaves 37% of rows unseen by each model), why
bagging reduces variance but not bias, why it therefore requires
low-bias, high-variance base models, the row/column/combination sampling
options, and the hyperparameters.

blocks.t: The Idea
From the notes

items: We chose low bias, high variance models (overfitting).

Thus we use bagging; the resulting model is LBLV — low bias,
 low variance — since data is sampled for each model.
Assumptions: all models are the same; models are LBHV.

So bagging reduces the variance, as impact is shared because of
 data sampling to each model.
Similarly for regression we take the mean.

blocks.cap:
The notes' diagram. The name is the two halves of the picture:
 Bootstrapping — sampling and training models on different datasets —
 followed by Aggregation.

blocks.t: Voting vs bagging — the one-line difference
Bootstrapping
Sampling with replacement

Draw $n$ rows from a dataset of $n$ rows with replacement. Some rows appear
several times; others not at all. The probability a given row is never drawn is
\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)^{n} \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} e^{-1}\approx0.368 .

So each model sees about 63% of the distinct rows, and roughly
37% are out-of-bag — unseen by that model. Those unseen rows are a
free validation set, which is Topic 62.

blocks.cap:
Left: three bootstrap samples of ten rows. Rows repeat, and each
 sample misses several. Right: the fraction never drawn converges to $1/e$
 regardless of dataset size.

blocks.t: The notes' 1500/500 example

The diagram shows 1500 rows with 500 sampled per model. Sampling fewer
rows than the dataset holds (max_samples < 1.0) increases diversity —
each model sees a more distinct slice — at the cost of each being individually
weaker. It is a hyperparameter; the scikit-learn default draws $n$ rows with
replacement.
Why It Reduces Variance
The formula, and what it implies
For $B$ models each with variance $\sigma^2$ and pairwise correlation $\rho$:

\operatorname{Var} \left(\frac1B\sum_b \hat f_b\right)
 =\rho\sigma^{2}+\frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^{2},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Bias} \left(\frac1B\sum_b \hat f_b\right)
 =\frac1B\sum_b\operatorname{Bias}(\hat f_b).
Two conclusions, and they dictate the whole design:

items:
Averaging reduces variance — the second term vanishes as $B$
 grows.

Averaging does nothing for bias — the bias of the average is
 the average of the biases.

blocks.t:
Therefore bagging can only help a model whose error is variance. That is
exactly the notes' assumption: the base models must be LBHV. Bagging a
high-bias model such as a stump changes almost nothing, because there is no
variance to remove.

blocks.cap:
One deep tree carves a jagged, over-fitted boundary. Averaging ten
 smooths it; averaging two hundred produces a boundary close to the truth —
 LBHV converted to LBLV, exactly as the notes say.

blocks.t: Why the trees inside a bag should NOT be pruned

A pruned tree has lower variance and higher bias. Bagging removes variance for
free but cannot remove bias, so pruning the base learners throws away the thing
bagging is good at and keeps the thing it cannot fix. Grow the trees
fully and let the averaging do the work — the opposite of the advice for a
single tree (Topic 57).
What Gets Sampled

head: Sampling
Parameter
Effect
rows: The classic form. Enables OOB scoring
Decorrelates further; essential in high dimensions

blocks.t:
Sampling columns as well as rows is what turns bagged trees into a
random forest — with one further refinement, that the column sampling
happens at every split rather than once per tree. That distinction is
Topic 61.
Properties

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Large variance reduction; strongly resists overfitting
Cannot reduce bias — useless on an underfitting model
Correlated base models cap the benefit
More models never hurts — $B$ is not a tuning risk
Little gain on stable learners such as linear regression

blocks.t: $B$ is the one hyperparameter you cannot set too high

Unlike depth or learning rate, increasing the number of estimators never causes
overfitting — the variance formula is monotonically decreasing in $B$. It only
costs time. Set it as high as your budget allows and tune the others; the curve
flattens once the $\rho\sigma^2$ floor is reached, typically well before 500
trees.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier, BaggingRegressor
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, LinearRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2000
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 12))
y = (X[:, 0] + .8*X[:, 1] - .5*X[:, 2] + .5*X[:, 0]*X[:, 1]
     + rng.normal(0, 1.1, n) > 0).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3,
                                          stratify=y, random_state=0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. BOOTSTRAP SAMPLING -- and the 1/e result
# =====================================================================
data = np.arange(10)
for s in range(3):
    samp = np.random.default_rng(s).integers(0, 10, 10)
    oob = sorted(set(data) - set(samp))
    print(f"sample {s}: {samp}  ->  {len(set(samp))} distinct, OOB = {oob}")

print(f"\n{'n':>7s} {'fraction OOB':>14s} {'theory (1-1/n)^n':>18s}")
for n_ in [5, 10, 50, 100, 1000, 10_000]:
    frac = np.mean([1 - len(set(np.random.default_rng(s).integers(0, n_, n_)))/n_
                    for s in range(200)])
    print(f"{n_:7d} {frac:14.4f} {(1-1/n_)**n_:18.4f}")
print(f"{'limit':>7s} {1/np.e:14.4f} {'1/e':>18s}")
# ~37% of rows are never drawn -- that is the out-of-bag set (Topic 62).

# =====================================================================
# 2. BAGGING FROM SCRATCH -- bootstrap, then aggregate
# =====================================================================
def bagging_fit(X, y, B=100, seed=0):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    models, oob_masks = [], []
    for b in range(B):
        idx = r.integers(0, len(X), len(X))          # BOOTSTRAP
        m = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=b).fit(X[idx], y[idx])
        models.append(m)
        mask = np.ones(len(X), bool); mask[np.unique(idx)] = False
        oob_masks.append(mask)                       # rows this model never saw
    return models, np.array(oob_masks)

def bagging_predict(models, X):
    votes = np.array([m.predict(X) for m in models])  # AGGREGATE
    return (votes.mean(axis=0) >= 0.5).astype(int)

models, oob = bagging_fit(X_tr, y_tr, B=100)
print(f"\nscratch bagging test accuracy: "
      f"{(bagging_predict(models, X_te) == y_te).mean():.4f}")
print(f"single tree test accuracy    : "
      f"{DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
print(f"average OOB fraction         : {oob.mean():.4f}")

sk = BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(), n_estimators=100,
                       random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"sklearn BaggingClassifier    : {sk.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. IT REDUCES VARIANCE, NOT BIAS
# =====================================================================
def bias_variance(make_model, sims=120):
    grid = rng.normal(0, 1, (300, 12))
    truth = (grid[:, 0] + .8*grid[:, 1] - .5*grid[:, 2] + .5*grid[:,0]*grid[:,1] > 0)
    preds = []
    for s in range(sims):
        Xi = rng.normal(0, 1, (400, 12))
        yi = (Xi[:, 0] + .8*Xi[:, 1] - .5*Xi[:, 2] + .5*Xi[:,0]*Xi[:,1]
              + rng.normal(0, 1.1, 400) > 0).astype(int)
        preds.append(make_model().fit(Xi, yi).predict(grid))
    P = np.array(preds)
    mean_pred = P.mean(axis=0)
    return np.mean((mean_pred - truth)**2), np.mean(P.var(axis=0))

print(f"\n{'base learner':30s} {'Bias^2':>9s} {'Variance':>10s}")
for tag, mk in [
    ("deep tree (LBHV)",      lambda: DecisionTreeClassifier()),
    ("bagged deep trees",     lambda: BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(),
                                                        n_estimators=50)),
    ("stump (HBLV)",          lambda: DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1)),
    ("bagged stumps",         lambda: BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1),
                                                        n_estimators=50)),
]:
    b2, v = bias_variance(mk)
    print(f"{tag:30s} {b2:9.4f} {v:10.4f}")
# Deep trees: variance COLLAPSES, bias barely moves -> big gain.
# Stumps:     variance was already low -> bagging buys almost nothing.
# THIS is why the notes require LBHV base models.

# =====================================================================
# 4. DO NOT PRUNE THE TREES INSIDE A BAG
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'base depth':>11s} {'single tree':>13s} {'bagged (200)':>14s}")
for d in [1, 3, 6, 12, None]:
    one = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=0),
                          X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean()
    bag = cross_val_score(BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d),
                                            n_estimators=200, random_state=0),
                          X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, n_jobs=-1).mean()
    print(f"{str(d):>11s} {one:13.4f} {bag:14.4f}")
# A SINGLE tree is best at moderate depth. A BAG is best with FULLY GROWN
# trees -- exactly the opposite of Topic 57's advice for one tree.

# =====================================================================
# 5. MORE MODELS NEVER HURTS
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'n_estimators':>13s} {'test accuracy':>15s}")
for B in [1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 300, 1000]:
    m = BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(), n_estimators=B,
                          random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"{B:13d} {m.score(X_te, y_te):15.4f}")
# Monotone improvement, then a plateau at the rho*sigma^2 floor.
# Unlike depth or learning rate, B cannot be set "too high".

# =====================================================================
# 6. WHAT GETS SAMPLED -- rows, columns, or both
# =====================================================================
variants = {
    "rows only (classic)":  dict(max_samples=1.0, max_features=1.0,
                                 bootstrap=True,  bootstrap_features=False),
    "columns only":         dict(max_samples=1.0, max_features=0.5,
                                 bootstrap=False, bootstrap_features=True),
    "both (random patches)":dict(max_samples=0.7, max_features=0.5,
                                 bootstrap=True,  bootstrap_features=True),
    "smaller row sample":   dict(max_samples=0.33, max_features=1.0,
                                 bootstrap=True,  bootstrap_features=False),
}
print(f"\n{'sampling':24s} {'cv accuracy':>13s}")
for tag, kw in variants.items():
    s = cross_val_score(BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(),
                                          n_estimators=100, random_state=0, **kw),
                        X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, n_jobs=-1).mean()
    print(f"{tag:24s} {s:13.4f}")
# Sampling COLUMNS as well as rows is the step towards a random forest (T61).

# =====================================================================
# 7. IT WORKS WITH ANY BASE LEARNER -- but only helps unstable ones
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'base learner':22s} {'alone':>8s} {'bagged':>9s} {'gain':>8s}")
for tag, base in [("decision tree", DecisionTreeClassifier()),
                  ("KNN (k=1)",     KNeighborsClassifier(1)),
                  ("KNN (k=50)",    KNeighborsClassifier(50)),
                  ("logistic reg",  LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))]:
    a = cross_val_score(base, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean()
    b = cross_val_score(BaggingClassifier(base, n_estimators=100, random_state=0),
                        X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, n_jobs=-1).mean()
    print(f"{tag:22s} {a:8.4f} {b:9.4f} {b-a:+8.4f}")
# Big gains for UNSTABLE learners (deep tree, 1-NN). Almost none for STABLE
# ones (50-NN, logistic regression) -- they had no variance to remove.

# =====================================================================
# 8. REGRESSION -- "similarly we take the mean"
# =====================================================================
yr = X[:, 0]*2 + X[:, 1] - .5*X[:, 2]**2 + rng.normal(0, 1, n)
Xr_tr, Xr_te, yr_tr, yr_te = train_test_split(X, yr, test_size=.3, random_state=0)

one = DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0).fit(Xr_tr, yr_tr)
bag = BaggingRegressor(DecisionTreeRegressor(), n_estimators=200,
                       random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(Xr_tr, yr_tr)
print(f"\nsingle tree R2 {one.score(Xr_te, yr_te):.4f}")
print(f"bagged      R2 {bag.score(Xr_te, yr_te):.4f}")

manual = np.mean([e.predict(Xr_te[:, f]) if f is not None else e.predict(Xr_te)
                  for e, f in zip(bag.estimators_, bag.estimators_features_)], axis=0)
print(f"the aggregate IS the mean: {np.allclose(manual, bag.predict(Xr_te))}")

# =====================================================================
# 9. PARALLEL BY CONSTRUCTION
# =====================================================================
import time
for jobs in [1, -1]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(), n_estimators=200,
                      random_state=0, n_jobs=jobs).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"n_jobs={jobs:3d}: {time.perf_counter()-t0:.2f}s")
# Every model is independent, so bagging parallelises perfectly.
# Boosting (Topic 65) cannot -- it is sequential by construction.
Worked Examples
What a bootstrap sample contains
Original dataset: 10 rows, indexed $0$ to $9$. A bootstrap sample draws 10 times with replacement.

items: Unique rows used: $\{0,1,2,3,5,7,9\}$, that is 7 distinct rows.
Row 7 appears three times; rows 4, 6 and 8 never appear.

blocks.t: Expected fraction of unique rows. The chance a given row is never drawn in $n$ draws is $(1-\tfrac1n)^n$:
P(\text{row not drawn}) = \left(\tfrac{9}{10}\right)^{10} = 0.349
So about $65\%$ of rows are expected in each bootstrap sample. For large $n$ this tends to $1-e^{-1} = 0.632$.

Why this matters. Each bagged model sees a different $\sim$63% of the data, so the models differ and their average has lower variance. The $\sim$37% left out are reused as a free validation set (out-of-bag evaluation, next chapter).
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Bagging $=$ Bootstrap AGGregatING: bootstrapping
 (sampling, and training models on different datasets) followed by
 aggregation.

Assumptions: all models are the same, and the models are LBHV
 (low bias, high variance).

We choose LBHV models — overfitting ones — and
 bagging makes the result LBLV, since data is sampled for each
 model.

Bagging reduces variance, as the impact of noisy points is shared
 because of the data sampling. It does not reduce bias — the
 bias of an average is the average of the biases.

Bootstrap sampling draws $n$ rows with replacement, so each model
 sees about 63% of the distinct rows and $\approx$37% are
 out-of-bag — a free validation set (Topic 62).

Do not prune the base trees. Grow them fully; the averaging
 removes the variance and nothing can remove added bias.

You can sample rows, columns, or both.
 Sampling columns too is the step towards a random forest.
Similarly for regression we take the mean.

More estimators never hurts — $B$ only costs time. Bagging is
 perfectly parallel; boosting is not.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. What does bagging stand for, and what are the two halves?

Bootstrap AGGregatING. First bootstrapping — draw $n$ rows with replacement for
each model, so every model trains on a different dataset. Then aggregation —
majority vote for classification, mean for regression.
Q. Why must the base models be high-variance?

Because averaging reduces variance but leaves bias untouched — the bias of an
average is the average of the biases. Bagging a high-bias model such as a stump
changes essentially nothing, since there was no variance to remove.
Q. Should you prune the trees inside a bagging ensemble?

No. Pruning trades variance for bias, and bagging removes variance for free while
being powerless against bias. Grow the trees fully — the exact opposite of the
advice for a single tree.
Q. What is the 37% figure?

The probability that a given row is never drawn in a bootstrap sample of size $n$
is $(1-1/n)^n \to 1/e \approx 0.368$. So each model never sees about 37% of the
rows, and those out-of-bag rows provide a free validation estimate (Topic 62).
Q. Can you set n_estimators too high?

No — the variance of the average decreases monotonically in $B$, so more models
never hurt accuracy. They only cost time and memory, and the curve flattens once
the correlation floor $\rho\sigma^2$ is reached.
Q. Why does bagging help a decision tree but not logistic regression?

Because logistic regression is a stable, low-variance learner — refit on a
bootstrap sample it gives nearly the same answer, so $\rho\approx1$ and averaging
achieves nothing. Deep trees and 1-NN are unstable, so their errors decorrelate
and cancel.
Q. Bagging or boosting?

Bagging when a single model overfits — it attacks variance and parallelises
perfectly. Boosting when a single model underfits — it attacks bias, but is
sequential and more sensitive to noise. That contrast is Topic 66.
